newsitem.title: USA: IMF endorses stepped-up aid for world's poor.
newsitem.headline: IMF endorses stepped-up aid for world's poor.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund on Wednesday endorsed stepped-up aid for the world's poorest nations, but stopped short of spelling out how it planned to pay for that.
The decision, announced by IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus, effectively left open the controversial question of whether the IMF would sell some of its gold to help the world's poor.
"The IMF is fully ready to assist its low-income members well into the next millenium," Camdessus said in a brief statement after a lengthy IMF board meeting.

Camdessus, backed by the United States, Britain and most other member nations, had proposed selling 5 million of the fund's 104 million ounces of gold if needed to help finance stepped-up assistance to poor countries.
But a few nations -- Germany, Italy and Switzerland -- opposed the proposal, arguing in part that the IMF should not sell gold except in cases of extreme financial emergency.

Camdessus said the board had reached "understandings" to ensure a permanent continuation of the IMF's Enhanced Structural Adjustment loan Facility (ESAF) and its participation in a multilateral debt relief plan for poor nations.
But he did not say how that would be accomplished and an IMF spokesman declined to elaborate.
ESAF, which lends money to the world's poorest countries at virtually no interest charge, faces a roughly $3.5 billion financing gap from the years 2000 to 2004.

Bilateral contributions from major countries are expected to fill at least some of that gap. But Camdessus and his allies have argued that would not be enough and that a modest amount of gold sales would be necessary.
Under their proposal, the IMF would use the income generated from investing the proceeds of the gold sales to help finance the ESAF.
"When you get finished with all the modalities, it's the only way to do this," U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin told reporters earlier on Wednesday while the IMF was still meeting.
This was the IMF's second meeting in less than a week to discuss ways to help the world's poorest countries. The board failed to reach a consensus on selling gold at a meeting on Friday.
Camdessus said the discussions had taken place in a "cooperative spirit."
Finance ministers and central bank chiefs that make up the IMF's policy-making Interim Committee are expected to discuss the gold sales question when they meet in Washington on Sept. 29.
But an explicit agreement looks unlikely at that time.
